prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and its realisation at fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye. After the full first-round exchange I tried again to find a flaw and the case holds on its merits. The idea is single and bounded: trapping many neutral atoms in a lattice at the magic wavelength so that the lattice light does not shift the clock transition, which removes the motional and light-shift limits that constrained earlier neutral-atom approaches. It was turned into clocks at fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and reproduced independently in several national laboratories, so the interpretation is stable. The consequences are already real: tests of fundamental constants and relativity, relativistic geodesy, and a route to redefining the second. The attribution is uncontested in a way no other shortlisted candidate matches: Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking strontium lattice clocks to record accuracy and stability. All eight round-1 files name the same pair. I note this convergence only as a cross-check; I would hold the position if only I held it. The citation I propose names the lattice concept and the 1e-18 realisation together, so that it is separated from the 2005 frequency-comb prize (a tool for counting optical frequencies) and from the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems (which touched ion clocks).
statement.case_against: The remaining reservation is novelty. Frequency combs (2005) and single-ion control (2012) lie close, ion clocks are a competing line with comparable accuracy, and Ye's programme is bound up with comb-linked comparisons. A critic can say a lattice-clock prize honours a superb refinement of precision metrology and not a new phenomenon. Other groups (Lemonde, Bloom and Ludlow, Takamoto, ion-clock programmes) are outside the credit, and earlier trapping ideas by Ido and Kimble are noted by Mehlig. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the full societal payoff is anticipated rather than formal. A two-person prize in precision measurement also leaves the larger condensed-matter candidates for later, and I cannot claim that the choice between a measurement advance and a new organising principle for a field is settled by argument alone.

responses.point: Kroll notes that, as two atomic physicists on the committee, he and I share a disciplinary lens and may overvalue a measurement result, so the case should be tested against colleagues outside AMO; he also flags his research stay in John Hall's laboratory for the chair.
responses.response: I accept the caution and have tried to apply it. Supporters from outside atomic physics (Danielsson, Mehlig, Pearce) also back B057, and Mehlig and Pearce moved to it from a different opening first choice after weighing the case, which is a better test than two AMO members agreeing. I agree with your own framing that this is an invention with a decisive experimental demonstration, not an accuracy increment, and that the citation should say so. On your Hall connection, my view is that it is not disqualifying: a research stay in the laboratory of a 2005 laureate is a connection to the earlier prize, not to Katori or Ye, and the novelty question is one the committee debates openly. I leave the recusal judgement to the chair, but I would not treat your support as compromised.

responses.point: Eriksson argues for B053 because topological insulators introduced a new organising principle (the Z2 invariant) for a whole field, whereas the lattice clock is the culmination of a longer line already recognised with combs and ion clocks. He accepts B057 as a good outcome and asks what would change his order.
responses.response: The organising-principle argument is serious and it is the reason B053 stays on my alternative list. Two points keep it second for me. First, the lattice clock is not simply the end of the comb and ion line: magic-wavelength trapping lets many neutral atoms be interrogated in parallel without trap-induced shifts, a different physical route, and the committee can say in a sentence what is new. Second, your own case-against shows that the B053 trio leaves out real contributors, and the third slot is a choice between Mele and Hasan or a choice of whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be set aside. I cannot see that a citation wording resolves that, since the HgTe prediction tested by Molenkamp's experiment is the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. If the committee could resolve the credit for B053 and wished to weight a new organising principle above a measurement advance, I would support Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, but I do not think that is the case this year.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from the cavity method to B057 but flags that earlier trapping ideas by Ido and Kimble, other lattice-clock groups and the timing relative to the redefinition of the second remain open.
responses.response: I agree that the Ido and Kimble work on trapping and light shifts should be acknowledged, and I think it is answered by the claim the citation makes: the proposal of the magic wavelength for a neutral-atom optical lattice clock and its realisation, not trapping in general. On timing, my answer to the chair's question is that the redefinition is neither a condition nor a reason to wait. The scientific achievement, 1e-18 accuracy reproduced across laboratories, is complete; the redefinition is a later metrological decision that depends on international comparisons and a choice among clock species, and a prize that waited for it would be tied to something outside the achievement itself. I would keep it out of the citation text.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from IceCube to B057, lists B054 as the fair alternative reading if a new observational window is valued over metrological precision, and says the credit split for other lattice-clock contributors cannot be verified.
responses.response: On B054 my position from round 1 stands: opening a new messenger is the kind of discovery a prize exists for, but isolating three names from a large collaboration with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors is hard, and source-level associations remain modest, so this year it is a reason to wait rather than to prefer it. Should the committee prefer B054, I would want the citation tied to the diffuse astrophysical flux. On your question about other lattice-clock contributors: I would not add a third name. Lemonde, Bloom and others made real contributions to the clock ecosystem, but I know of no documented claim that matches the concept-plus-record structure of Katori and Ye, and a third name would be an arbitrary choice that weakens the clean credit rather than improving it.

responses.point: Danielsson says breadth of opening support should not decide between B057 and B053, because the B053 attribution problem is harder, and lists the 2016 topological-phase prize overlap.
responses.response: I agree that breadth of support must not decide it, and I have tried not to use it. The weight against B053 for me is the contested credit and the partial overlap with the 2016 prize, not a count of rankings. I would add that the five top-three placements it received come from members whose fields differ, so if the committee were to set B057 aside, B053 is where I would expect the discussion to go, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the defensible core if the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan were explained in the citation and accepted.

uncertainties: How much weight the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 prizes should carry in judging novelty; I think the lattice concept is distinct enough, but this is a judgement the committee cannot settle with data.
Whether two names are fully adequate given the contributions of other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups; I see no documented third claim of the same kind.
Whether the committee should treat the not yet decided redefinition of the second as irrelevant to timing, as I do, or as a reason to wait.
For B053, whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan can be defended in a public citation if the committee turns to the alternative.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I have a long-running scientific collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, papers with the Lund attosecond group, work with Ursula Keller's ETH group, and work with Reinhold Schuch, Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato; none of these people is credited on the shortlist. B057 and B005 lie in my broader field of atomic physics, so I disclose subfield closeness, as the chair has recorded, but my profile documents no connection to Katori or Ye and no specific conflict is apparent. Having read Kroll's disclosure about John Hall, I note that I have no documented tie to Hall either.
